Coffee’s relationship to type 2 diabetes risk is actively debated. Large prospective studies and meta-analyses report that habitual coffee drinkers have a lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes, with risk reductions increasing with more cups per day [d2,d5]. These sources attribute potential benefits to coffee’s polyphenols and minerals that may improve insulin sensitivity [d2,d3,d4,d5]. In contrast, other evidence notes that caffeine can acutely raise blood sugar and that adding sweeteners or dairy to coffee can increase insulin resistance and diabetes risk [d1,d3]. Because outcomes depend on preparation and individual metabolism, the evidence supports conflicting opinions rather than a single definitive answer [d1,d2,d3,d4,d5,d6,d7].
